title: Western tradition, African music and departure and return
summary: The I-IV-V as departure and return, and the Oliver Nelson story.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young

blocks.x: I don't think you would have jazz as we know it without
No, because we are western Europe.

There's an interesting story. Oliver Nelson, around 1969 or so, did a tour of Africa with a seven or eight piece band and he said, it's an interesting thing that you have in African music some very sophisticated things about it, melodies, rhythms.
Sure, sure. Which are now ours, because the world is no longer regional.

Sure. But he said on the other hand those people harmonically can't hear, if you go from a I chord to a IV chord, because-- which is something so basic to western music in general, and in to jazz in particular as far as say for example the blues, but he says they just don't hear that, because they're not geared towards harmonic thinking.

That's right. But to me, the whole concept of I, IV, V is symbolic. If you take it literal you're in trouble. It does have a basic meaning and I'm sure it's in African music too. It's the whole statement of departure and return and that trilogy, Father, Son and Holy Ghost, if you like, is basic to anything you can find, really. It effects movies this way; it gives that dimension to poetry, when poetry is read. The basis of musical formula is departure and return, basis, departure and coming back.
It's any form. It's how you do it. That's oversimplifying it, but that's exactly what it is
as many means of accomplishing that as there are people who account to it.
